problems.solution: Parametrize by \((y,z)\): \(\vec r_y \times \vec r_z = \langle 1, 2y, 2z\rangle\) has positive \(x\)-component, but we want the \(-x\) orientation, so use \(-\langle 1, 2y, 2z\rangle\). \[\vec F \cdot (-\langle 1, 2y, 2z\rangle) = -(x-4) - 2yz + 2yz = 4 - x = y^2 + z^2.\]Over \(D = \{y^2 + z^2 \le 6\}\), in polar: \(I = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{\sqrt 6}\rho^3\, d\rho\, d\theta = 2\pi\cdot 9 = 18\pi\).

problems.problem: Evaluate \( \displaystyle \iint\limits_{S}{{\vec F\centerdot \,d\vec S}}\) where \(\vec F = \,\vec i + 4z\,\vec j + \left( {z - y} \right)\,\vec k\) and \(S\) is the portion of \(y = 4z + {x^3} + 6\) that lies over the region in the xz-plane with bounded by \(z = {x^3}\), \(x = 1\) and the x-axis oriented in the positive \(y\)-axis direction.
problems.solution: Parametrize by \((x,z)\): \(\vec r_x \times \vec r_z = \langle 3x^2, -1, 4\rangle\) has negative \(y\)-component, so for the \(+y\) orientation use \(\langle -3x^2, 1, -4\rangle\). \[\vec F \cdot \langle -3x^2, 1, -4\rangle = -3x^2 + 4z - 4(z - y) = -3x^2 + 4y = -3x^2 + 4(4z + x^3 + 6).\]Integrate over \(0 \le x \le 1\), \(0 \le z \le x^3\): \[I = \int_0^1 \int_0^{x^3}(-3x^2 + 16z + 4x^3 + 24)\, dz\, dx = \int_0^1 (12x^6 - 3x^5 + 24x^3)\, dx = \frac{101}{14}.\]

problems.problem: Evaluate \( \displaystyle \iint\limits_{S}{{\vec F\centerdot \,d\vec S}}\) where \(\vec F = \left( {x + y} \right)\,\vec i + x\,\vec j + z{x^2}\,\vec k\) and \(S\) is the portion of \({x^2} + {y^2} = 36\) between \(z = - 3\) and \(z = 1\) oriented outward (i.e. away from the \(z\)-axis).
problems.solution: On the cylinder \(x = 6\cos\theta, y = 6\sin\theta\), the outward normal is \(\vec r_\theta \times \vec r_z = \langle 6\cos\theta, 6\sin\theta, 0\rangle\). Then \[\vec F\cdot (\vec r_\theta \times \vec r_z) = (x + y)(6\cos\theta) + x(6\sin\theta) = 36\cos^2\theta + 72\sin\theta\cos\theta.\]Integrating over \(\theta \in [0, 2\pi]\) gives \(36\pi\); integrating over \(z \in [-3, 1]\) (length 4) gives \(I = 4\cdot 36\pi = 144\pi\).

problems.problem: Evaluate \( \displaystyle \iint\limits_{S}{{\vec F\centerdot \,d\vec S}}\) where \(\vec F = z\,\vec i + 3\,\vec k\) and \(S\) is the portion of \({x^2} + {y^2} + {z^2} = 4\) with \(z \ge 0\) oriented outwards (i.e. away from the origin).
problems.solution: On the upper hemisphere of radius 2, the outward normal element is \(\vec r_\varphi \times \vec r_\theta = 4\sin\varphi\,\langle \sin\varphi\cos\theta, \sin\varphi\sin\theta, \cos\varphi\rangle\). With \(\vec F = \langle z, 0, 3\rangle = \langle 2\cos\varphi, 0, 3\rangle\), \[\vec F \cdot (\vec r_\varphi \times \vec r_\theta) = 8\sin^2\varphi\cos\varphi\cos\theta + 12\sin\varphi\cos\varphi.\]The first term vanishes (\(\int_0^{2\pi}\cos\theta\, d\theta = 0\)); the second gives \(12\cdot 2\pi\cdot \tfrac{1}{2} = 12\pi\).

problems.problem: Evaluate \( \displaystyle \iint\limits_{S}{{\vec F\centerdot \,d\vec S}}\) where \(\vec F = - x\,\vec i + \left( {4 + y} \right)\,\vec j - z\,\vec k\) and \(S\) is the portion of \({x^2} + {z^2} = 9\) between \(y = 2\) and \(y = 10 - x\) oriented inward (i.e. towards from the \(y\)-axis).
problems.solution: Parametrize \(\vec r(\theta, y) = \langle 3\cos\theta, y, 3\sin\theta\rangle\). Then \(\vec r_\theta \times \vec r_y = \langle -3\cos\theta, 0, -3\sin\theta\rangle\), pointing toward the \(y\)-axis (inward) — the requested orientation. \[\vec F\cdot (\vec r_\theta \times \vec r_y) = 3x\cos\theta + 3z\sin\theta = 9\cos^2\theta + 9\sin^2\theta = 9.\]With \(y \in [2, 10 - 3\cos\theta]\), \(I = \int_0^{2\pi} 9(8 - 3\cos\theta)\, d\theta = 9\cdot 16\pi = 144\pi\).

problems.problem: Evaluate \( \displaystyle \iint\limits_{S}{{\vec F\centerdot \,d\vec S}}\) where \(\vec F = y\,\vec i + 2\,\vec j + {\left( {z + 3} \right)^2}\,\vec k\) and \(S\) is the surface of the solid bounded by \(z = 2{x^2} + 2{y^2} - 3\) and \(z = 1\) with the negative orientation. Note that both surfaces of this solid are included in \(S\).
problems.solution: Apply the Divergence Theorem with a sign flip for the inward (\"negative\") orientation. \(\operatorname{div}\vec F = 0 + 0 + 2(z+3)\). The solid \(E\) has \(z \in [2\rho^2 - 3,\, 1]\), \(\rho \in [0, \sqrt 2]\). The inner \(z\)-integral of \(2(z+3)\) gives \((z+3)^2\big|_{2\rho^2-3}^{1} = 16 - 4\rho^4\). Then \[\iiint_E \operatorname{div}\vec F\, dV = 2\pi\int_0^{\sqrt 2}(16 - 4\rho^4)\rho\, d\rho = 2\pi\cdot \frac{32}{3} = \frac{64\pi}{3}.\]With negative orientation, \(I = -\tfrac{64\pi}{3}\).

problems.problem: Evaluate \( \displaystyle \iint\limits_{S}{{\vec F\centerdot \,d\vec S}}\) where \(\vec F = \left( {x - y} \right)\,\vec i + z\,\vec j + y\,\vec k\) and \(S\) is the surface of the solid bounded by \({y^2} + {z^2} = 4\), \(x = y - 3\), and \(x = 6 - z\) with the positive orientation. Note that all three surfaces of this solid are included in \(S\).
problems.solution: By the Divergence Theorem: \(\operatorname{div}\vec F = 1\), so \(I = \iiint_E dV = \text{vol}(E)\). The solid is the cylinder \(y^2 + z^2 \le 4\) with \(y - 3 \le x \le 6 - z\). \[\text{vol}(E) = \iint_{y^2+z^2\le 4}(9 - y - z)\, dA = 9\cdot 4\pi = 36\pi,\]since \(y\) and \(z\) integrate to 0 by symmetry. So \(I = 36\pi\).

problems.problem: Evaluate \( \displaystyle \iint\limits_{S}{{\vec F\centerdot \,d\vec S}}\) where \(\vec F = y\,\vec i - 2\,\vec k\) and \(S\) is the portion of the sphere of radius 1 with \(z \ge 0\) and \(x \le 0\) with the positive orientation. Note that all three surfaces of this solid are included in \(S\).
problems.solution: Per the note, \(S\) is the full boundary of the quarter-ball \(\{x^2+y^2+z^2 \le 1,\, z \ge 0,\, x \le 0\}\): the spherical cap plus the two flat disks in \(x = 0\) and \(z = 0\). Compute the divergence: \(\operatorname{div}\vec F = \partial(y)/\partial x + 0 + \partial(-2)/\partial z = 0\). By the Divergence Theorem, \[\iint_S \vec F \cdot d\vec S = \iiint_E 0\,dV = 0.\]

problems.problem: Evaluate \( \displaystyle \iint\limits_{S}{{\vec F\centerdot \,d\vec S}}\) where \(\vec F = 3x\,\vec i + 2z\,\vec j + \left( {1 - {y^2}} \right)\vec k\) and \(S\) is the portion of \(z = 2 - 3y + {x^2}\) that lies over the triangle in the xy-plane with vertices \(\left( {0,0} \right)\), \(\left( {2,0} \right)\) and \(\left( {2, - 4} \right)\) oriented in the negative \(z\)-axis direction.
problems.solution: Parametrize by \((x,y)\): \(\vec r_x \times \vec r_y = \langle -2x, 3, 1\rangle\) has positive \(z\)-component. For the \(-z\) orientation, use \(\langle 2x, -3, -1\rangle\). \[\vec F\cdot \langle 2x, -3, -1\rangle = 6x^2 - 6z + y^2 - 1 = y^2 + 18y - 13\quad\text{after substituting }z.\]On the triangle (\(0\le x\le 2,\, -2x\le y\le 0\)): \[I = \int_0^2 \int_{-2x}^0 (y^2 + 18y - 13)\, dy\, dx = \int_0^2 \left(\tfrac{8x^3}{3} - 36x^2 - 26x\right)\, dx = -\frac{412}{3}.\]

problems.problem: Evaluate \( \displaystyle \iint\limits_{S}{{\vec F\centerdot \,d\vec S}}\) where \(\vec F = - x\,\vec i + 2y\,\vec j - z\,\vec k\) and \(S\) is the portion of \(y = 3{x^2} + 3{z^2}\) that lies behind \(y = 6\) oriented in the positive \(y\)-axis direction.
problems.solution: Parametrize by \((x,z)\): \(\vec r_x \times \vec r_z = \langle 6x, -1, 6z\rangle\) has negative \(y\)-component. For \(+y\) orientation use \(\langle -6x, 1, -6z\rangle\). Then \[\vec F\cdot \langle -6x, 1, -6z\rangle = 6x^2 + 2y + 6z^2 = 6(x^2 + z^2) + 6(x^2 + z^2) = 12(x^2 + z^2).\]Over \(D = \{x^2 + z^2 \le 2\}\), in polar: \(I = 12\cdot 2\pi\int_0^{\sqrt 2}\rho^3\, d\rho = 24\pi\cdot 1 = 24\pi\).

problems.problem: Evaluate \( \displaystyle \iint\limits_{S}{{\vec F\centerdot \,d\vec S}}\) where \(\vec F = {x^2}\,\vec i + 2z\,\vec j - 3y\,\vec k\) and \(S\) is the portion of \({y^2} + {z^2} = 4\) between \(x = 0\) and \(x = 3 - z\) oriented outwards (i.e. away from the \(x\)-axis).
problems.solution: Parametrize \(\vec r(\theta, x) = \langle x, 2\cos\theta, 2\sin\theta\rangle\). The outward normal \(\vec r_\theta \times \vec r_x = \langle 0, 2\cos\theta, 2\sin\theta\rangle\) points away from the \(x\)-axis. Then \[\vec F\cdot \vec n = 4z\cos\theta - 6y\sin\theta = 8\sin\theta\cos\theta - 12\cos\theta\sin\theta = -4\sin\theta\cos\theta = -2\sin(2\theta).\]With \(x \in [0, 3 - 2\sin\theta]\), \(I = \int_0^{2\pi}-2\sin(2\theta)(3 - 2\sin\theta)\, d\theta\). Both pieces integrate to 0 over \([0, 2\pi]\), so \(I = 0\).

problems.problem: Evaluate \( \displaystyle \iint\limits_{S}{{\vec F\centerdot \,d\vec S}}\) where \(\vec F = \,\vec i + z\,\vec j + 6x\,\vec k\) and \(S\) is the portion of the sphere of radius 3 with \(x \le 0\), \(y \ge 0\) and \(z \ge 0\) oriented inward (i.e. towards the origin).
problems.solution: On the sphere of radius 3, the inward normal element is \(-9\sin\varphi\,\langle \sin\varphi\cos\theta, \sin\varphi\sin\theta, \cos\varphi\rangle\). The octant \(x\le 0, y\ge 0, z\ge 0\) gives \(\varphi\in[0,\pi/2]\), \(\theta\in[\pi/2,\pi]\). With \(\vec F = \langle 1, z, 6x\rangle\), \[\vec F\cdot \vec n = -9\sin^2\varphi\big[\cos\theta + 3\cos\varphi\sin\theta + 18\cos\varphi\cos\theta\big].\]Integrating term by term: \(\int_{\pi/2}^{\pi}\cos\theta\, d\theta = -1\), \(\int_{\pi/2}^{\pi}\sin\theta\, d\theta = 1\), \(\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^2\varphi\, d\varphi = \pi/4\), \(\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^2\varphi\cos\varphi\, d\varphi = 1/3\). Combining: \(I = -9(-\pi/4 + 1 - 6) = 9\pi/4 + 45\).

problems.problem: Evaluate \( \displaystyle \iint\limits_{S}{{\vec F\centerdot \,d\vec S}}\) where \(\vec F = y\,\vec i + 2x\,\vec j + \left( {z - 8} \right)\,\vec k\) and \(S\) is the surface of the solid bounded by \(4x + 2y + z = 8\), \(z = 0\), \(y = 0\) and \(x = 0\) with the positive orientation. Note that all four surfaces of this solid are included in \(S\).
problems.solution: By the Divergence Theorem, since \(\operatorname{div}\vec F = 1\): \(I = \iiint_E dV = \text{vol}(E)\). The tetrahedron has vertices \((0,0,0),(2,0,0),(0,4,0),(0,0,8)\): \[\text{vol}(E) = \frac{1}{6}|2\cdot 4\cdot 8| = \frac{32}{3}.\]

problems.problem: Evaluate \( \displaystyle \iint\limits_{S}{{\vec F\centerdot \,d\vec S}}\) where \(\vec F = yz\,\vec i + x\,\vec j + 3{y^2}\,\vec k\) and \(S\) is the surface of the solid bounded by \({x^2} + {y^2} = 4\), \(z = x - 3\), and \(z = x + 2\) with the negative orientation. Note that all three surfaces of this solid are included in \(S\).
problems.solution: By the Divergence Theorem: \(\operatorname{div}\vec F = \frac{\partial(yz)}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial(x)}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial(3y^2)}{\partial z} = 0 + 0 + 0 = 0\). The flux through the closed surface (either orientation) is \(\iiint_E 0\, dV = 0\).

17.5.title: Stokes' Theorem
17.5.unitTitle: Conservative Fields, Green's, Stokes' & Divergence Theorems

problems.problem: Use Stokes’ Theorem to evaluate \( \displaystyle \iint\limits_{S}{{{\mathop{\rm curl}\nolimits} \vec F\centerdot d\vec S}}\) where \(\vec F = {x^3}\,\vec i + \left( {4y - {z^3}{y^3}} \right)\,\vec j + 2x\,\vec k\) and \(S\) is the portion of \(z = {x^2} + {y^2} - 3\) below \(z = 1\) with orientation in the negative \(z\)-axis direction.
problems.solution: By Stokes' Theorem, \(\iint_S \operatorname{curl}\vec F\cdot d\vec S = \oint_{\partial S}\vec F\cdot d\vec r\). The boundary is the circle \(x^2 + y^2 = 4,\, z = 1\). With \(S\) oriented in the \(-z\) direction, by the right-hand rule the boundary is traversed clockwise as seen from above: \(\vec r(t) = \langle 2\cos t,\, -2\sin t,\, 1\rangle\). Then \[\vec F(\vec r(t))\cdot \vec r'(t) = -16\sin t\cos^3 t + 16\sin t\cos t - 16\sin^3 t\cos t.\]Each term integrates to 0 over \([0, 2\pi]\) (each is of the form \(\sin^a t \cos^b t\) with at least one odd power, periodic), so \(I = 0\).

problems.problem: Use Stokes’ Theorem to evaluate \( \displaystyle \iint\limits_{S}{{{\mathop{\rm curl}\nolimits} \vec F\centerdot d\vec S}}\) where \(\vec F = 2y\,\vec i + 3x\,\vec j + \left( {z - x} \right)\,\vec k\) and \(S\) is the portion of \(y = 11 - 3{x^2} - 3{z^2}\) in front of \(y = 5\) with orientation in the positive \(y\)‑axis direction.
problems.solution: The boundary of \(S\) in \(y = 5\) is \(x^2 + z^2 = 2\). With \(+y\) orientation, the right-hand rule gives the boundary parametrization \(\vec r(t) = \langle \sqrt 2\cos t,\, 5,\, \sqrt 2\sin t\rangle\). Then \[\vec F(\vec r(t))\cdot \vec r'(t) = -10\sqrt 2\sin t + 2\sin t\cos t - 2\cos^2 t.\]Integrating over \([0, 2\pi]\): the first two terms vanish; the last gives \(-2\pi\). So \(I = -2\pi\).

problems.problem: Use Stokes’ Theorem to evaluate \( \displaystyle \iint\limits_{S}{{{\mathop{\rm curl}\nolimits} \vec F\centerdot d\vec S}}\) where \(\vec F = y\,\vec i - x\,\vec j + y{x^3}\,\vec k\) and \(S\) is the portion of the sphere of radius 4 with \(z \ge 0\) and the upwards orientation.
problems.solution: The boundary is \(x^2 + y^2 = 16\) at \(z = 0\). With upward orientation, the boundary is CCW from above: \(\vec r(t) = \langle 4\cos t, 4\sin t, 0\rangle\). \[\vec F\cdot \vec r' = (4\sin t)(-4\sin t) + (-4\cos t)(4\cos t) + 0 = -16(\sin^2 t + \cos^2 t) = -16.\]\(I = \int_0^{2\pi}(-16)\, dt = -32\pi.\)

problems.problem: Use Stokes’ Theorem to evaluate \( \displaystyle \iint\limits_{S}{{{\mathop{\rm curl}\nolimits} \vec F\centerdot d\vec S}}\) where \(\vec F = \left( {{z^2} - 1} \right)\,\vec i + \left( {z + x{y^3}} \right)\,\vec j + 6\,\vec k\) and \(S\) is the portion of \(x = 6 - 4{y^2} - 4{z^2}\) in front of \(x = - 2\) with orientation in the negative \(x\)-axis direction.
problems.solution: Compute \(\operatorname{curl}\vec F = \langle -1,\, 2z,\, y^3\rangle\). The boundary of \(S\) is \(y^2 + z^2 = 2\) in the plane \(x = -2\). Replace \(S\) with the disk \(D\) in this plane (same boundary), which simplifies the surface integral. To match the \(-x\) orientation, take \(\vec n = \langle -1, 0, 0\rangle\) on \(D\). Then \(\operatorname{curl}\vec F\cdot \vec n = (-1)(-1) = 1\), and \[\iint_S \operatorname{curl}\vec F\cdot d\vec S = \iint_D 1\, dA = \pi(\sqrt 2)^2 = 2\pi.\]

17.6.title: Divergence Theorem
17.6.unitTitle: Conservative Fields, Green's, Stokes' & Divergence Theorems

problems.problem: Use the Divergence Theorem to evaluate \( \displaystyle \iint\limits_{S}{{\vec F\centerdot d\vec S}}\) where \(\vec F = \left( {3x - z{x^2}} \right)\,\vec i + \left( {{x^3} - 1} \right)\,\vec j + \left( {4{y^2} + {x^2}{z^2}} \right)\,\vec k\) and \(S\) is the surface of the box with \(0 \le x \le 1\), \( - 3 \le y \le 0\) and \( - 2 \le z \le 1\). Note that all six sides of the box are included in \(S\).
problems.solution: \(\operatorname{div}\vec F = (3 - 2xz) + 0 + 2x^2 z = 3 + 2xz(x - 1)\). Over the box \([0,1]\times[-3,0]\times[-2,1]\) (volume 9): \[\iiint_E 3\, dV = 27,\quad \iiint_E 2xz(x-1)\, dV = 2\left(\int_0^1 x(x-1)\, dx\right)\left(\int_{-3}^0 dy\right)\left(\int_{-2}^1 z\, dz\right) = 2\cdot\left(-\tfrac{1}{6}\right)(3)\left(-\tfrac{3}{2}\right) = \tfrac{3}{2}.\]Sum: \(I = 27 + \tfrac{3}{2} = \tfrac{57}{2}\).

problems.problem: Use the Divergence Theorem to evaluate \( \displaystyle \iint\limits_{S}{{\vec F\centerdot d\vec S}}\) where \(\vec F = 4x\,\vec i + \left( {1 - 6y} \right)\,\vec j + {z^3}\,\vec k\) and \(S\) is the surface of the sphere of radius 2 with \(z \ge 0\), \(y \le 0\) and \(x \ge 0\). Note that all four surfaces of this solid are included in \(S\).
problems.solution: \(\operatorname{div}\vec F = 4 - 6 + 3z^2 = -2 + 3z^2\). The solid is one octant of the ball of radius 2: spherical \(\rho\in[0,2]\), \(\varphi\in[0,\pi/2]\), \(\theta\in[-\pi/2, 0]\), with volume \(4\pi/3\). \[\iiint_E -2\, dV = -\frac{8\pi}{3},\qquad \iiint_E 3z^2\, dV = 3\int_0^2 \rho^4\, d\rho \int_0^{\pi/2}\cos^2\varphi\sin\varphi\, d\varphi \int_{-\pi/2}^0 d\theta = 3\cdot\tfrac{32}{5}\cdot\tfrac{1}{3}\cdot\tfrac{\pi}{2} = \tfrac{16\pi}{5}.\]Sum: \(I = -\tfrac{8\pi}{3} + \tfrac{16\pi}{5} = \tfrac{8\pi}{15}\).

problems.problem: Use the Divergence Theorem to evaluate \( \displaystyle \iint\limits_{S}{{\vec F\centerdot d\vec S}}\) where \(\vec F = - xy\,\vec i + \left( {z - 1} \right)\,\vec j + {z^3}\,\vec k\) and \(S\) is the surface of the solid bounded by \(y = 4{x^2} + 4{z^2} - 1\) and the plane \(y = 7\). Note that both of the surfaces of this solid included in \(S\).
problems.solution: \(\operatorname{div}\vec F = -y + 3z^2\). The solid is bounded by the paraboloid (axis along \(y\)) with cross-section \(x^2 + z^2 \le 2\) and \(y\in[4(x^2+z^2)-1,\, 7]\). Use cylindrical \(x = \rho\cos\theta, z = \rho\sin\theta\). \[\iiint_E -y\, dV = \pi\int_0^{\sqrt 2}\big[16\rho^4 - 8\rho^2 - 48\big]\rho\, d\rho = -\frac{104\pi}{3},\]\[\iiint_E 3z^2\, dV = \pi\cdot \int_0^{\sqrt 2} 12\rho^3(2 - \rho^2)\, d\rho = 8\pi.\]Sum: \(I = -\tfrac{104\pi}{3} + 8\pi = -\tfrac{80\pi}{3}\).

problems.problem: Use the Divergence Theorem to evaluate \( \displaystyle \iint\limits_{S}{{\vec F\centerdot d\vec S}}\) where \(\vec F = \left( {4x - {z^2}} \right)\,\vec i + \left( {x + 3z} \right)\,\vec j + \left( {6 - z} \right)\,\vec k\) and \(S\) is the surface of the solid bounded by the cylinder \({x^2} + {y^2} = 36\) and the planes \(z = - 2\) and \(z = 3\) . Note that both of the surfaces of this solid included in \(S\).
problems.solution: \(\operatorname{div}\vec F = 4 + 0 - 1 = 3\). The solid is a cylinder of radius 6 and height 5: \(\text{vol}(E) = 36\pi\cdot 5 = 180\pi\). \[I = 3\cdot 180\pi = 540\pi.\]

problems.problem: Use the Divergence Theorem to evaluate \( \displaystyle \iint\limits_{S}{{\vec F\centerdot d\vec S}}\) where \(\vec F = y{x^2}\,\vec i + \left( {x{y^2} - 3{z^4}} \right)\,\vec j + \left( {{x^3} + {y^2}} \right)\,\vec k\) and \(S\) is the surface of the sphere of radius 4 with \(z \le 0\) and \(y \le 0\). Note that all three surfaces of this solid are included in \(S\).
problems.solution: \(\operatorname{div}\vec F = 2xy + 2xy + 0 = 4xy\). In spherical coordinates over the quarter-ball \(z\le 0, y\le 0\) (so \(\varphi\in[\pi/2,\pi]\), \(\theta\in[\pi, 2\pi]\)), \(4xy = 2\rho^2\sin^2\varphi\sin(2\theta)\). \[\iiint_E 4xy\, dV = 2\int_\pi^{2\pi}\sin(2\theta)\, d\theta\cdot \int_{\pi/2}^\pi\sin^3\varphi\, d\varphi\cdot \int_0^4 \rho^4\, d\rho.\]The first factor is \(0\), so \(I = 0\).

problems.problem: Use the Divergence Theorem to evaluate \( \displaystyle \iint\limits_{S}{{\vec F\centerdot d\vec S}}\) where \(\vec F = \sin \left( {\pi x} \right)\,\vec i + z{y^3}\,\vec j + \left( {{z^2} + 4x} \right)\,\vec k\) and \(S\) is the surface of the box with \( - 1 \le x \le 2\), \(0 \le y \le 1\) and \(1 \le z \le 4\). Note that all six sides of the box are included in \(S\).
problems.solution: \(\operatorname{div}\vec F = \pi\cos(\pi x) + 3zy^2 + 2z\). Over the box \([-1, 2]\times[0, 1]\times[1, 4]\) (volume 9): \[\iiint \pi\cos(\pi x)\, dV = \pi\int_{-1}^2 \cos(\pi x)\, dx \cdot 1 \cdot 3 = 0,\]\[\iiint 3zy^2\, dV = 3\cdot 3\cdot \tfrac{1}{3}\cdot \tfrac{15}{2} = \tfrac{45}{2},\qquad \iiint 2z\, dV = 6\cdot \tfrac{15}{2} = 45.\]Sum: \(I = 0 + \tfrac{45}{2} + 45 = \tfrac{135}{2}\).

problems.problem: Use the Divergence Theorem to evaluate \( \displaystyle \iint\limits_{S}{{\vec F\centerdot d\vec S}}\) where \(\vec F = 2xz\vec i + \left( {1 - 4x{y^2}} \right)\,\vec j + \left( {2z - {z^2}} \right)\,\vec k\) and \(S\) is the surface of the solid bounded by \(z = 6 - 2{x^2} - 2{y^2}\) and the plane \(z = 0\) . Note that both of the surfaces of this solid included in \(S\).
problems.solution: Compute the divergence: \(\partial(2xz)/\partial x = 2z\), \(\partial(1 - 4xy^2)/\partial y = -8xy\), \(\partial(2z - z^2)/\partial z = 2 - 2z\), so \(\operatorname{div}\vec F = 2 - 8xy\). The solid \(E\) is bounded above by the paraboloid \(z = 6 - 2x^2 - 2y^2\) and below by \(z = 0\); in cylindrical, \(\rho \in [0, \sqrt{3}]\), \(z \in [0, 6 - 2\rho^2]\), and \(\text{vol}(E) = 9\pi\). By the Divergence Theorem, \[\iint_S \vec F \cdot d\vec S = \iiint_E (2 - 8xy)\,dV = 2\,\text{vol}(E) - 8\iiint_E xy\,dV.\]The \(xy\) integral vanishes by symmetry (\(\int_0^{2\pi}\cos\theta\sin\theta\,d\theta = 0\)), so \(I = 2\cdot 9\pi = 18\pi.\)
